work.title: LuckyDomains.io: off Wix, onto a site the company owns
work.summary: The company site moved from Wix to a hand-built static site on GitHub Pages, with the duplicate-URL problems fixed and every decision written down in a public repository.
work.problem: The old site ran on Wix. It was small and dated, and it carried a recurring subscription for capability the business was not using. The owner wanted a site that was portable, versioned, and editable by coding agents.
work.approach: Rebuild as plain static HTML with no framework and no build step, served from GitHub Pages on the company's own domain. Fix duplicate URLs with canonical tags and consistent internal links, because a static host cannot write server redirects.
done: Moved the site from Wix to GitHub Pages on the apex domain, with HTTPS
Rewrote 93 internal links to one canonical form
Gave every page a self-referencing canonical tag that matches the sitemap
Kept old .html addresses as noindex stubs that point to the new URLs
Shared one Person identifier for the founder with kenashe.ai
Added a dependency-free test suite that runs on every push
lessons: On a static host, canonical tags and consistent internal links do the job redirects cannot.
Blocking duplicate URLs in robots.txt backfires: a blocked page cannot be crawled, so its canonical tag is never read.
Writing decisions down makes the next change faster, whether a person or an agent makes it.
work.noMetrics: No traffic, ranking, or lead figures are claimed for this project.
work.built: Built and deployed with an AI agent, with the decisions recorded in the repository.

Decision D11: old .html addresses stay as small noindex pages that point to the new URL, because a static host cannot redirect.
Decision D8: a dependency-free test suite runs on every push, checking links, canonicals, the sitemap, and metadata.

websites.lead: You do not just need a website that looks good. You need the owned foundation that search visibility, brand authority, and AI recognition depend on. Lucky Domains designs and builds it on your own domain.
intro: A good-looking site can still be invisible. Most of the problems we see are structural: pages that do not match what people search for, slow templates, duplicate URLs, missing structured data, and content no one can find from the home page.
We fix that at the foundation. Information architecture comes before visual design, and the technical work is built in from the first template, not added after launch.

faq: Do you redesign existing sites or only build new ones?
Both. Ken starts by reviewing the site you have and writes down what is holding it back. Sometimes the right answer is to fix it. Sometimes it is to rebuild.
Which platform do you build on?

Whatever you can maintain. LuckyDomains.io is plain static HTML on GitHub Pages because that suits a small site. Larger sites may need a content management system. The recommendation comes with the scope.
Will the new site keep my search rankings?

A redesign is planned so existing URLs keep working: redirects or canonicals for anything that moves, and a check of what Google has indexed before launch. No one can guarantee rankings, but a careful migration protects what you have.
Do you write the content?
Ken plans the page structure around real search demand and drafts or edits core page copy with you. You stay the source of facts about your business.

faq: Is SEO still worth it with AI search?

Yes. Google says its AI features are built on its core search systems and that the same SEO fundamentals apply. Pages that are crawlable, useful, and well structured are the ones AI features can draw on.
How long does SEO take?
Technical fixes can show up within weeks. Content and authority take months. The work is cumulative, which is why it is scoped as ongoing.
Do you build links?
No rented or bought links. Authority comes from earned, editorial references and content worth citing.

faq: Can you get my business recommended by ChatGPT?
No one can promise that. What can be done is to make the evidence about your business clear, consistent, and easy to verify, so systems that look for it find it.
Is this different from SEO?

It builds on SEO. Crawlable pages, good content, and accurate structured data are the foundation. AI visibility adds entity consistency, third-party corroboration, and testing how AI systems actually describe you.
Do I need an llms.txt file or special AI markup?
Google says its search features do not use them and that no special markup is needed. Other services may. Lucky Domains will tell you which, if any, are worth maintaining for your situation.

entity.title: Entity SEO & Digital Identity
entity.h1: Help search engines and AI systems understand exactly who you are.
entity.lead: Search engines increasingly organize the web around entities, not just keywords. Lucky Domains helps people and companies create a clear, consistent identity across their website, structured data, profiles, and credible third-party sources.
what: Traditional SEO helps pages rank. Entity SEO helps search engines understand the person or organization behind those pages: the canonical website, official profiles, founders, companies, authors, credentials, products, and credible references that all belong to the same real-world entity.
When those signals conflict or stay disconnected, systems struggle to tell one person or company from another. When they are consistent and machine-readable, they have a clearer picture to work with.

entity.panel: Google creates Knowledge Panels automatically. No one can submit a form to force one. This work improves the evidence Google uses to recognize an entity and tell it apart from everyone with a similar name.

What is an entity home?
The one page that says, authoritatively, who you are: usually your homepage or founder page, with structured data that the rest of the web can point to.

domains.anchor: Domains already work as identity anchors for people, companies, products, and online properties. Email, profiles, citations, and structured data all point back to the name.

faq: How much does it cost to buy a domain that is not for sale?
It depends on the name, its history, and the owner. Ken sets a fair-market range from comparable sales before anyone is contacted, and you approve or decline every price.
Will the owner know who I am?
No. Outreach is anonymous so the price stays grounded in value, not in how well funded the buyer looks.
What if the owner will not sell?
Some will not. Ken tells you plainly and stops, rather than pushing toward a number that only makes sense to the seller.

buy.title: How We Buy Domains
buy.h1: How we buy a domain that is not listed for sale
buy.lead: Most good .coms are registered and not for sale. That does not mean they cannot be bought. It means the buyer needs a number, a method, and patience. Here is exactly what Ken does when a client wants a name someone else owns.

steps.name: Set the range
steps.line: Before anyone is contacted, Ken builds a fair-market range for the name from comparable sales, traffic and keyword data, and what the domain is strategically worth to your business. You see that range and the reasoning behind it.

steps.name: Reach the owner anonymously
steps.line: Ken identifies the registrant and opens the conversation without revealing who the buyer is. A price should reflect what the asset is worth, not how well funded the buyer looks.

steps.name: Negotiate against the range
steps.line: Sellers open high. Ken negotiates against the range you agreed, not against the opening ask, and tells you plainly if the owner's price moves outside what the name is worth to you.

article.title: Can domains become the identity layer for AI agents?
article.dek: People use domains as durable identities. Businesses use them as the canonical home of their brand. AI agents may need something similar: a readable name, a way to be found, and a way to check who stands behind them.
sections: Domains already do this for people and companies

A domain is the one identifier most people and businesses fully control. Email, profiles, structured data, and citations all point back to it. When a search engine or an AI system needs to decide which company a mention belongs to, the domain is often the anchor that settles it.

An agent that offers a service, or pays for one, needs some of the same things: a human-readable name, a known place to be looked up, a description of what it does that other software can read, a payment destination tied to that name, evidence that a result came from it, and a record that travels with it.
What Ken has tested in public

ZeroHuman is a small service that sells two jobs to other AI agents. Its ENS name, zerohuman.eth, is the storefront, the payment address, and the sender of every result. A text record on the name publishes the menu, and the service is listed in the ERC-8004 agent registry as agent #56626, linked back from the name with an ENSIP-25 record.
An earlier experiment had two AI agents with their own wallets complete one purchase on Ethereum mainnet, with an ENS text record as the storefront. Both are documented on KenAshe.ai.

As of November 20, 2026, no outside agent had bought from ZeroHuman. Both experiments were operated by Ken. There is no settled standard for agent identity, and these tests are evidence that the pieces can work, not that the market has chosen them.

This is research, not a product. Lucky Domains does not sell agent identity. The question matters to the core work anyway: if software is going to look businesses up, the same identity signals that help search engines and AI systems today will matter even more.
